query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled mild oxidative post‐treatment of the near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst will induce a selective, in situ exsolution of an amorphous, porous oxide layer (enriched in Cu/Ni active sites) that stabilizes the active redox couple and oxygen vacancies. This surface reconstruction will lower the light‐off temperature for CO/hydrocarbon oxidation, enhance resistance to H2O/NO poisoning, and improve long‐term structural durability under transient automotive exhaust conditions—all while maintaining low platinum-group-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst containing predominantly earth‐abundant metals (e.g. Cu, Ni, etc.) with trace amounts of PGMs.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, mild oxidative thermal treatment (e.g., exposing the catalyst to air or a low‐oxygen environment at moderate temperatures around 300–500 °C for a set period) to trigger selective surface exsolution and form a porous, oxide-rich shell.
generation.conditions: Testing under simulated transient automotive exhaust conditions with fluctuating temperatures (from ~80 °C up to 300 °C), in the presence of typical poisoning species (H2O vapor, NO, and other exhaust gases), and under cyclic thermal/operational stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a hierarchically porous oxide shell (with a high density of oxygen vacancies and stabilized Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox sites) that is embedded on the original high-entropy alloy framework.
generation.mechanism: The mild oxidative treatment promotes controlled exsolution of a thin, porous oxide layer from the alloy surface without triggering bulk phase separation. This layer—by virtue of its higher configurational entropy and tailored oxygen vacancy concentration—enhances the Mars–van Krevelen oxidation pathway (thus lowering activation temperatures) and minimizes strong adsorption of poisoning species (H2O, NO). Meanwhile, the porous structure acts as a barrier against sintering and degradation during thermal cycling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated catalyst, the post-treated material is expected to exhibit a significant decrease (e.g., >50 °C reduction) in the light-off temperature for CO oxidation, improved resistance against deactivation by H2O and NO under transient conditions, and minimal performance drop during extended simulated aging (over hundreds of hours).
generation.baseline: The unmodified near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst without the oxidative treatment, which under similar test conditions shows higher light‐off temperatures, faster degradation due to sintering and phase rearrangement, and a greater susceptibility to poisoning by moisture and NO.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective under realistic, transient automotive exhaust conditions (moderate temperatures and common poisons) but may not be sufficient if the catalyst is exposed to extreme thermal regimes (e.g., above 900 °C) or if uncontrolled oxidation leads to structural collapse.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from studies on Pt/HEO nanofibers (e.g., PMC12224923::web::021 and PMC12224923::web::004) and rock-salt HEOs (e.g., PMC8007101::web::012) supports the benefit of stabilizing redox-active sites via a high-entropy effect and porous architectures, the ability to reproducibly control the extent of exsolution and prevent adverse structural collapse (as warned in PMC12224923::web::018) in a complex, multi-element alloy remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the same near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst; subject one batch to the mild oxidative thermal treatment (300–500 °C in an air or low‐O2 atmosphere for a predetermined time) and leave the other untreated. Evaluate both catalysts under simulated automotive exhaust conditions that include temperature transients, periodic exposure to moisture (10 vol% H2O) and NO, and accelerated aging (thermal cycling up to 700 °C over 300 hours). Compare the light-off curves for CO oxidation, poisoning resistance (e.g., under repeated cycles with H2O/NO), and post-ageing structural characterization (using techniques such as HAADF–STEM and XPS).
measurements: Light‐off temperature (T10 and T50) for CO oxidation
Rate of deactivation under cyclic exposure to H2O and NO (activity vs time)
Post-aging structural integrity and porosity (via HAADF–STEM, XRD, and BET surface area)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidative treatment does not lead to a statistically significant reduction in light‐off temperatures, fails to improve resistance to H2O/NO poisoning, or results in comparable or worsened long-term degradation relative to the untreated catalyst, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The size of Pt nanoparticles on HEO‐P only slightly increased in the entire heating process. During high‐temperature aging, the relatively low surface energy at the grain boundary (GB) of the HEO causes Pt nanoparticles to spontaneously migrate toward the GB (Figure 3d).[  ] This diffusion may lead to encounters between individual Pt nanoparticles, resulting in their aggregation into larger nanoparticles. For HEO‐P, the rise in temperature causes the structural collapse somehow. The diminished GB in turn compromises the stability of the Pt nanoparticles. These findings highlight the significant role of the pore structure within HEO nanofibers in suppressing Pt nanoparticle sintering, offering a promising strategy for designing sinter‐resistant nanocatalysts leveraging the high‐entropy effect (Figure 3e).

cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation.
